newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk minister rules out IMF stand-by accord.
newsitem.headline: Turk minister rules out IMF stand-by accord.

text.p: Turkish State Minister Ufuk Soylemez on Friday ruled out the possibility of a stand-by accord with the International Monetary Fund during current talks with the organistaion.

"At this stage there is no question of signing something like a stand-by accord in the context of this visit," Soylemez, who is responsible for the Treasury and privatisation, told journalists before talks with an IMF delegation.
Turkish officials had already indicated there were no plans for such an agreement during regular annual consultations with the IMF group, led by Martin Hardy, which began this week.
Turkish markets and political leaders are looking to the IMF's two-week visit for some glimmer of support for the government's economic policies.

"We can say that in principle a medium-term programme may be under consideration," Soylemez said, adding that details could not be disclosed. He added that the high level of inflation necessitated the development of such a medium-term programme.

The State Institute of Statistics announced on Friday that Turkey's wholesale prices rose 6.0 percent in March and 77.0 percent year-on-year. Consumer prices were up 5.4 percent and 77.3 percent respectively.
Soylemez forecast a clear improvement in the inflation situation from April.
Turkey was to present to the IMF delegation evidence of improvements in the economy achieved by the Islamist-led government since it came to power nine months ago, Soylemez said.

He pointed to the lengthening of domestic debt maturities to an average of 13 months from 4.5 months a year ago, to a fall in interest rates to 95 percent from 140 percent and to the rise in foreign reserves to $16 billion from $12-13 billion over the same period.
Soylemez said after talks with the delegation that the IMF "looked warmly" on the idea of a medium-term programme.
Hardy said any accord would depend on the government's plans.

"We have said many times we believe Turkey has very strong potential and we are very confident that these discussions will be fruitful in terms of a better understanding of how the government is going to move forward in the coming year," he said.

Economic analysts say the coalition between the Islamist Welfare Party of Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan and the conservative True Path Party (DYP) of pro-western Tansu Ciller is too occuped with political concerns to address the underlying causes of runaway inflation and yawning public deficits.
